comments.text:
Having worked on a brand book for a high-end  hotel brand and having a father whose company's franchised hotel was found not adhering to Sheraton brand guidelines (it later became a Crowne Plaza), I have a tip for travellers: when you complain online about a hotel, don't say a waiter was rude to you, or a pillow wasn't fluffed enough, first say that your stay doesn't meet expectations of the brand. It will scare the bejesus out of them. Have receipts: say that x-hotel-chain's brand guidelines specify metal cutlery at breakfast but you were given plastic cutlery. If you don't want to research brand guidelines, use your own knowledge: you have stayed in four Aubergine Rocket hotels. You go to one Aubergine Rocket hotel which doesn't have the neon Aubergine Rocket logo behind the check-in desk, and has shorter breakfast time, say it doesn't meet your expectations based on previous experience of the brand.
A real bugbear for me is international airport hotels that don't have 24/7 facilities.  You arrive from a delayed flight at 1am and are told you can't get a beer and a club sandwich. **** that!

comments.author: @Lefty3333
comments.text:
This is all very poorly researched.  The majority of properties in North America are franchise owned and franchise managed.  The parent company, in the example given around the three minute mark with Hilton, has no clue or say in the handbook/work rules/benefits - or lack of them - that the franchisee offers.  How could they?  It's the franchisee's hotel, not Hilton's. You're not a Hilton employee, you're an employee of xyz franchisee. Sure, if this is one of the rare unicorn scenarios where Hilton actually managed/owns the property (never with an HGI) then yes, they dictate all of things mentioned.  But in reality, employees can be sitting on chairs at the front desk if the franchise owner/management company/local management allow it, you are allowed to solicit for tips via QR codes if the same people I mentioned prior allow it just like you can't if they won't.

What's not brought up is the fact that in the asset light model that all of the parent brands have endorsed, overall, they are have no clue what goes on at the properties on a day to day basis and how could they?  Usually each property is getting a QA audit once a year.  So one day a year, the parent brand puts boots on the ground.  What happens the other 364 days a year?  Very few people fill out guest surveys which is the other main tool used.  Overall, things are taken almost on the honor system, that the franchisees are "doing the right thing."

The real thing to remember is this.  The parent company loves the appearance of standards because it helps their top line.  The franchisee, spends all of their time trying to bend/push/sabotage those standards because it helps their bottom line.

comments.text:
Having worked in the hotel industry, what's funny is that I can tell you with absolute certainty that he could have done this exact video for Hilton and literally all he would have had to do was replace the Marriott brand names with the Hilton brand names. He could have left the rest of the script exactly the same. 
These are two massive corporations, each with thousands of hotels among dozens of brands, but they have copied each others homework so much that they are effectively identical from an outside perspective.
Franchising fees and other associated costs are really the only thing that matter at the end of the day, since either one will be able to offer a franchisee pretty much the same package - it's all about which one is willing to go lower or offer cheaper overhead options.
Can't speak for any of the other corporations, since I don't have any experience with them, but I assume the story is the same.
